chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter is a journey through five ideas: counting in groups, landmark numbers, a base, place value and zero. Each number system is used, not just looked at: students write numbers in it, add in it and find where it breaks, so that the next idea arrives as the fix for a real difficulty.

points.title: Use each system before judging it
points.text: Every system is met through writing and adding numbers in it, and its weakness is found by trying a number it cannot handle.

points.title: Tools only where handling is the idea
points.text: Nine tools, each used once: matching sticks to tally marks, building names and Roman numerals, reading Egyptian symbols, grouping counters into a base, regrouping on a counting board, a base 60 place board, holding an empty place, and sorting number systems by their features.

points.title: Our own symbols for strange numerals
points.text: Picture numerals are always read back into Hindu numerals with the grouping written out, so the structure is clear even when the symbols are new.

points.title: History as a story, not a list
points.text: Reema and her father carry the story; dates and names are context, and the chapter keeps asking what problem each new idea solved.

concepts.concept_name: A loose page of strange symbols

content.text:
3.1 Reema's Curiosity
One lazy afternoon, Reema was flipping through an old book when, whoosh!, a piece of paper slipped out and floated to the floor. She picked it up and stared at the strange symbols all over it. "What is this?" she wondered.
She ran to her father, holding the paper as if it were a secret treasure. He looked at it and smiled. "Around 4000 years ago, there flourished a civilisation in a region called Mesopotamia, in the western part of Asia, containing a major part of the present-day Iraq and a few other neighbouring countries. This is one of the ways they wrote their numbers!"
Reema's eyes lit up, "Seriously? These strange symbols were numbers?"
Since when have humans been counting? What was their need for counting? What were they counting?
Since when have people been writing numbers in the modern form?
How would the Mesopotamians have written 20? 50? 100?

content.text:
Humans had the need to count even as early as the Stone Age. They were counting to determine the quantity of food they had, the number of animals in their livestock, details regarding trades of goods, the number of offerings given in rituals, etc.
Ancient Indian texts, such as the Yajurveda Samhita, mentioned names of numbers based on powers of 10, almost as we say them orally today. For example, they listed names for the numbers one (eka), ten (dasha), hundred (shata), thousand (sahasra), ten thousand (ayuta), etc., all the way up to 10 to the power 12 and beyond.
The first known instance of numbers being written using ten digits, including the digit 0 (which was then notated as a dot), occurs in the Bakhshali manuscript (c. 3rd century CE).
The Indian number system was transmitted to the Arab world by around 800 CE.
From the Arab world, the Hindu numerals were transmitted to Europe and to parts of Africa by around 1100 CE.
"The ingenious method of expressing every possible number using a set of ten symbols (each symbol having a place value and an absolute value) emerged in India." (Pierre-Simon Laplace)
The most commonly used terminologies for the numbers we use today are 'Hindu numerals', 'Indian numerals', and the transitional 'Hindu-Arabic numerals'.
The shape of the digits 0, 1, 2, ..., 9 used to write numbers in the Indian number system today evolved over a period of time.

content.text:
Worked example: The Yajurveda lists eka, dasha, shata, sahasra and ayuta. Which numbers are these, and how is each one related to the one before it?
1. eka is one and dasha is ten: 10 × 1 = 10.
2. shata is a hundred: 10 × 10 = 100.
3. sahasra is a thousand: 10 × 100 = 1000.
4. ayuta is ten thousand: 10 × 1000 = 10000.
5. Each name is 10 times the one before it, so the names follow powers of 10, just as we say numbers today.
Answer: 1, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000; each is 10 times the one before

concepts.concept_name: One stick for every cow: one-to-one mapping

content.text:
The Mechanism of Counting
Imagine that we are living in the Stone Age, say, around ten thousand years ago. Suppose we have a herd of cows.
Q1. How do we ensure that all cows have returned safely after grazing? Q2. Do we have fewer cows than our neighbour? Q3. If there are fewer, how many more cows would we need so that we have the same number of cows as our neighbour?
Method 1: We could tackle the questions by using pebbles, sticks or any object that is available in abundance. Let us choose sticks. For every cow in the herd, we could keep a stick.
This way of associating each cow with a stick, such that no two cows are associated or mapped to the same stick is called a one-to-one mapping.
How will you use such sticks to answer the other two questions (Q2 and Q3)?

content.text:
1. Predict first: with no number names at all, can you tell whether every cow came home?
2. Keep one stick for each cow in the morning. In the evening, take one stick out for each cow that returns.
3. A stick left over means a cow is missing; this pairing, one cow to one stick, is a one-to-one mapping.
4. To compare with a neighbour, pair your sticks with theirs: the unpaired sticks show who has more and how many more are needed.

content.text:
Worked example: In the morning a herder keeps one stick for each cow. In the evening she takes out one stick for each cow that returns, and 2 sticks are left. Her neighbour's stick bundle, paired stick by stick with hers, has 3 sticks without partners. What can she say?
1. Each returning cow removes exactly one stick, so every stick left stands for a cow that did not return.
2. 2 sticks are left, so 2 cows are still missing.
3. Pairing her sticks with the neighbour's sticks one to one, the 3 unpaired sticks are on the neighbour's side.
4. So she has fewer cows than her neighbour, and she needs 3 more cows to have the same number.
Answer: 2 cows are missing; she has fewer cows than her neighbour and needs 3 more

concepts.concept_name: A number system is a standard sequence

content.text:
For counting and finding the size of a collection, we need a standard sequence of objects, or names, or written symbols, that has a fixed order. Let us call this standard sequence a number system.
Since there is no end to numbers, the challenge is to come up with an unending standard sequence/number system that is easy to count with.
Using sticks gives an unending standard sequence/number system. However, it is not convenient to count larger collections, as we will need as many sticks as the number of objects being counted.
The standard sequence/number system given in Method 3 was actually the system used in Europe before it got replaced by the Hindu number system. It is called the Roman number system.
The symbols occurring in a written number system are called numerals.

3. Roman symbols: compact, but bigger and bigger numbers keep needing new symbols.
4. None of the three is both unending and easy; that is the challenge a good number system must meet.

content.text:
Figure it Out (the mechanism of counting, question 1): Suppose you are using the number system that uses sticks to represent numbers, as in Method 1. Without using either the number names or the numerals of the Hindu number system, give a method for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing two numbers or two collections of sticks.
1. To add, put the two collections of sticks together; the joined pile is the sum.
2. To subtract, pair each stick of the smaller pile with a stick of the larger pile and take the pairs away; the unpaired sticks are the difference.
3. To multiply, lay out the first pile once for every stick of the second pile and join all the copies.
4. To divide, keep taking out groups the size of the second pile; the number of groups is the quotient and the sticks that cannot make a full group are the remainder.
Answer: Add by joining, subtract by pairing and removing, multiply by repeating one pile once per stick of the other, divide by taking out equal groups

Figure it Out (the mechanism of counting, question 2): One way of extending the number system in Method 2 is by using strings with more than one letter, for example, we could use 'aa' for 27. How can you extend this system to represent all the numbers? There are many ways of doing it!
1. After z, start again with doubled letters: aa, bb, cc, ..., zz count the next 26 objects.
2. Then use tripled letters aaa, bbb, ..., zzz for the next 26, and so on.
3. Another way: after z use aa, ab, ac, ..., az, then ba, bb, ..., like the columns of a spreadsheet.
4. Either way, longer strings can always be made, so the sequence never runs out.
Answer: One way: a to z, then aa, bb, ..., zz, then aaa, bbb, ..., zzz and so on; many other ways work

3.2 Some Early Number Systems
I. Use of Body Parts: Many groups of people across the world have used their hands and body parts for counting.
II. Tally Marks on Bones and Other Surfaces: One of the oldest methods of number representation is by making notches, marks cut on a surface such as a bone or a wall of a cave. These marks are also called tally marks.
In this method, a mark is made for each object that is being counted.
The Lebombo bone, discovered in South Africa, is an even older tally stick with 29 notches, estimated to be around 44,000 years old.

content.text:
Worked example: The Lebombo bone has 29 notches. Group them in fives. How many full groups are there, and how many notches are left over?
1. Count off five notches at a time: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
2. That is 5 full groups of five, and 5 × 5 = 25.
3. 29 − 25 = 4, so 4 notches are left over.
4. So the 29 notches read as 5 groups of five and 4 more: 5 × 5 + 4 = 29.
Answer: 5 groups of five and 4 more

A group of indigenous people in Australia called the Gumulgal had the following words for their numbers: 1 urapon, 2 ukasar, 3 ukasar-urapon, 4 ukasar-ukasar, 5 ukasar-ukasar-urapon, 6 ukasar-ukasar-ukasar.
The numbers are counted in 2s, using which the number names are formed: 3 = 2 + 1, 4 = 2 + 2, 5 = 2 + 2 + 1, 6 = 2 + 2 + 2.
Gumulgal called any number greater than 6 ras.
Despite being so far apart geographically, and with no trace of contact between them, these three groups have developed equivalent number systems!

concepts.concept_name: Grouping by one size, and its limit

content.text:
A general form which this idea has taken in different number systems is as follows: count in groups of a certain number (like 2 in the case of Gumulgal's system), and use the word or symbol associated with this group size to represent bigger numbers.
Some of the commonly used group sizes in different number systems have been 2, 5, 10 and 20.
Up to what group size could you immediately see the number of objects without counting? Most humans find it difficult to count groups having 5 or more objects in a single glance.
What could be the difficulties with using a number system that counts only in groups of a single particular size? How would you represent a number like 1345 in a system that counts only by 5s?

Worked example: In a system that counts only by 5s, how would 1345 be written? How many group symbols are needed?
1. Find how many fives make 1345: 1345 ÷ 5 = 269.
2. Check: 269 × 5 = 1345, so nothing is left over.
3. So 1345 needs the symbol for five written 269 times.
4. That is far too many symbols to write or read, so a single group size soon becomes cumbersome.

Figure it Out (early number systems, question 1): A group of indigenous people in a Pacific island use different sequences of number names to count different objects. Why do you think they do this?
1. Think about what was being counted: fish, coconuts, canoes, days.

3. A separate sequence also tells the listener what kind of object is meant.
4. So the sequences may follow how each kind of object is usually grouped, traded or used.

Students explain how the Gumulgal names for 3 to 6 are built from urapon (1) and ukasar (2), and build the name for a number up to 6.
Students find the group size they can see at a glance, explain why tally marks were bunched in fives, and show that counting 1345 in fives alone still needs 269 groups.
Students explain why some people use different counting sequences for different objects, and add, subtract, multiply and divide numbers written in the Gumulgal system extended beyond 6.

content.text:
Figure it Out (early number systems, question 2): Consider the extension of the Gumulgal number system beyond 6 in the same way of counting by 2s. Come up with ways of performing the different arithmetic operations (+, −, ×, ÷) for numbers occurring in this system, without using Hindu numerals. Use this to evaluate the following: (i) (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) + (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) (ii) (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) − (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar) (iii) (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) × (ukasar-ukasar) (iv) (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar) ÷ (ukasar-ukasar)
1. (i) Join the words: 4 ukasar and 3 ukasar give 7 ukasar, and the two urapons make one more ukasar, so 8 ukasar. Check: 9 + 7 = 16.
2. (ii) Take 3 ukasar away from 4 ukasar and an urapon: ukasar-urapon is left. Check: 9 − 6 = 3.
3. (iii) ukasar-ukasar is two twos, so write the first number two times and then double the result, 4 copies in all: 16 ukasar and 4 urapons, and the 4 urapons make 2 more ukasar, so 18 ukasar. Check: 9 × 4 = 36.
4. (iv) Share 8 ukasar into groups of ukasar-ukasar: there are 4 groups, written ukasar-ukasar. Check: 16 ÷ 4 = 4.
Answer: (i) ukasar written 8 times (ii) ukasar-urapon (iii) ukasar written 18 times (iv) ukasar-ukasar

concepts.concept_name: Group a number into landmark numbers

content.text:
IV. The Roman Numerals
To get the Roman numeral for any number till 39, it is first grouped into as many 10s as possible, the remaining is grouped into as many 5s as possible, and finally the remaining is grouped into 1s.
Example: Let us take the number 27. 27 = 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1. So, 27 in Roman numerals is XXVII.
Instead of representing 50 as XXXXX, a new symbol is given to it: L. Following the way the number 4 is represented as 1 less than 5, that is, as IV, 40 is represented as 10 less than 50, that is, as XL.
Let us call all these numbers that have a new basic symbol as landmark numbers.
I 1, V 5, X 10, L 50, C 100, D 500, M 1,000.
Consider the number 2367. Writing it as a sum of landmark numbers starting from 1000 such that we take as many 1000s as possible, 500s as possible, and so on, we get 2367 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1.
This system seems to have evolved out of the ancient Greek number system in around the 8th century BCE in Rome, and evolved over time.

content.text:
Worked example: Write 2367 as a sum of Roman landmark numbers and then as a Roman numeral.
1. Two 1000s fit in 2367: 2367 − 2000 = 367. No 500 fits in 367.
2. Three 100s fit: 367 − 300 = 67. One 50 fits: 67 − 50 = 17.
3. One 10 fits: 17 − 10 = 7. One 5 fits: 7 − 5 = 2, which is two 1s.
4. So 2367 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1.
5. Writing one symbol for each landmark, 2367 is written as MMCCCLXVII.
Answer: 2367 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1, written as MMCCCLXVII

Despite the relative efficiency of the Roman system, it doesn't lend itself to an easy performance of arithmetic operations, particularly multiplication and division.
Example: Try adding the following numbers without converting them to Hindu numerals: (a) CCXXXII + CCCCXIII
Let us find the total number of Is, Xs, and Cs, and group them starting from the largest landmark number.
Apparently, it looks like the largest landmark number is C, but note that 5 Cs (100s) make a D (500).
The efficiency of this system is due to the grouping of a given number by not just one group size, but a sequence of group sizes that we call landmark numbers.

Worked example: Find V × L, L × D, V × D and VII × IX in Roman numerals.
1. V × L is 5 × 50 = 250, which is 100 + 100 + 50, written as CCL.
2. L × D is 50 × 500 = 25000, which is 25 thousands, written as M repeated 25 times.
3. V × D is 5 × 500 = 2500, which is 1000 + 1000 + 500, written as MMD.
4. VII × IX is 7 × 9 = 63, which is 50 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1, written as LXIII.
5. None of these products is a single landmark symbol, so there is no simple rule.
Answer: V × L is CCL, L × D is 25 M's, V × D is MMD and VII × IX is LXIII

content.text:
Figure it Out (Roman numerals, question 1): Represent the following numbers in the Roman system. (i) 1222 (ii) 2999 (iii) 302 (iv) 715
1. (i) 1222 = 1000 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 1 + 1, written as MCCXXII.
2. (ii) 2999 = 1000 + 1000 + 900 + 90 + 9; 900 is CM, 90 is XC and 9 is IX, so it is written as MMCMXCIX.
3. (iii) 302 = 100 + 100 + 100 + 1 + 1, written as CCCII.
4. (iv) 715 = 500 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 5, written as DCCXV.
Answer: (i) MCCXXII (ii) MMCMXCIX (iii) CCCII (iv) DCCXV

tool_config.idea: A Roman numeral groups a number into landmark numbers 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000, largest first, and adds their values. A smaller symbol written before a larger one is subtracted, so IV is 4 and XC is 90.
tool_config.screen: A target number at the top, a tray of landmark tiles I, V, X, L, C, D and M, a build row where tiles are placed left to right, and a running total under the row that updates as each tile is placed.
student_does: Read the target number and split it into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones.
Drag landmark tiles into the build row, largest first.
Use a subtractive pair such as CM, XC or IV where four of a symbol would be needed.
Check the running total against the target and read the finished numeral back.

feedback: A wrong total shows each tile's value under it, so the stray tile is easy to see.
Four of the same tile in a row is flagged and the subtractive pair is suggested.
A subtractive pair that the Romans did not use, such as IC, is rejected with the reason.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students write a number as a sum of the Roman landmark numbers, taking as many of the largest as possible first, and turn the sum into a Roman numeral such as MMCCCLXVII for 2367.
Students add two Roman numerals without converting them, by counting each symbol and regrouping five I's into V, five C's into D and so on, as in CCXXXII + CCCCXIII.
Students add LXXXVII and LXXVIII by counting L's, X's, V's and I's and regrouping each step into the next landmark.
Students multiply pairs of Roman landmark numbers, find that some products such as L × D have no single symbol, and explain why Roman numerals make multiplication hard.
Students write numbers in Roman numerals, list the features that make the Hindu number system more efficient than the Roman system, and refine a number system of their own.

content.text:
Figure it Out (early number systems, question 3): Identify the features of the Hindu number system that make it efficient when compared to the Roman number system.
1. Place value: in our numerals the position of a digit tells its landmark, so ten digits write every number; Roman symbols have fixed values and need new symbols for bigger numbers.
2. Zero: we have a digit 0 for an empty place; the Roman system has no symbol for zero.
3. Calculation: adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing follow simple column rules in our system, while Roman numerals make them very hard.
Answer: Place value with ten digits, a symbol for zero, and easy calculation
